Hear you are: Teaching LLMs Spatial Reasoning with Vision and Spatial Sound

                                 Hyeonggon Ryu1                    Joon Son Chung2           David Harwath3
      1
          Hankuk University of Foreign Studies 2 Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
                                     3
                                       The University of Texas at Austin
                      Where's my phone?                 Ah,                                                    Hmm, someone
                     Could you call it for me?   it's in my bag!                                               over there asked
                                                                                                               a question...




                                                                                  I have a
                                                                                 question!




Figure 1. Audio-Visual Spatial Reasoning. (Left) A phone rings out of sight inside a bag; although the sound’s semantic cue (“ring tone”)
is present, spatial reasoning is required to locate the true source among visually silent objects. (Right) In a classroom, several students
share the same semantic cue (“speech”), so the teacher must rely on spatial audio to identify which student asked the question. These
examples illustrate that accurate audio-visual understanding demands not only semantic alignment but also spatial comprehension.

                            Abstract                                         1. Introduction

Many audio-visual learning methods have focused on align-                    We live in a world full of sights and sounds, naturally asso-
ing audio and visual information, either through semantic                    ciating what we hear with what we see. Several cues help
or temporal correspondence. However, most of these works                     us connect the two, such as the visual appearance and au-
have utilized monaural audio, which does not contain in-                     dible characteristics of an object, the synchronization be-
formation about the spatial location of the sound source. In                 tween an action or event and its corresponding sound, and
contrast, humans and other animals utilize binaural hear-                    the direction from which the sound arrives, through bin-
ing to perceive this spatial information. Combining spatial                  aural hearing. We rely on these audio-visual cues to lo-
sound and visual perception enables powerful high-level                      cate a missing mobile device, or to know when an emer-
reasoning: for example, a person looking for their phone                     gency vehicle is approaching as we are driving. This nat-
may hear the ringing sound coming from a backpack sitting                    ural ability to connect auditory and visual information has
on a table, and quickly infer that the missing phone is in-                  motivated advancements in audio-visual machine learning,
side the backpack. In this paper, we investigate the problem                 such as sound source localization (object detection based

sual signals is absent but spatial alignment exists, as well as              commonly use monaural audio, focus on the semantic cor-
cases with multiple audio-visual semantic correspondences                    respondence between a sound and the visual appearance of
that require spatial reasoning to disambiguate. We propose                   the object that made the sound, or the audio-visual temporal

thesize the spatial sound question answering dataset with

a 10-second audio binaural waveform sampled at 32 kHz.
